processing: Described as a blend of mature new tea with aged tea, pressed as a seven-son style cake; the exact recipe is not published.
harvest_season: Not sold by picking: it is a factory blend, and the batch and date on the wrapper mark production.
appearance_dry: A pressed round cake; little is documented beyond the dark leaf typical of Menghai ripe tea.
appearance_liquor: Typical of ripe pu-erh: deep red-brown.
appearance_wet: Typical of ripe pu-erh: soft, dark brown leaf.
taste_profile: Described as fairly mellow with an aged aroma and a returning sweetness. The name means roughly 'strongest flavour', though there is little independent tasting to back that up.

brewing.notes: General ripe pu-erh approach: one quick rinse, water near the boil, short early steeps; add time gradually after the fourth steep.

vintage_note: Sold as a cake marked with production batch and date. Release history is thin, so judge a given cake by those details and its storage, as with other factory ripe teas.
description:
Wei Zui Yan is a Dayi ripe cake whose name promises the strongest flavour, 酽 being the Chinese word for thick, strong tea. It is a less documented cake than the factory's numbered classics.

A retail account describes it as a blend of mature new tea with aged tea. That fits its description as mellow, though the proportions are not published.

The reported cup is gentle with an aged aroma and a returning sweetness. Tasting notes are few and mostly commercial, so take them lightly. Brew as you would other ripe Menghai tea.

Check batch and date when buying, and note the alternative character 釅 on some listings, which is the same name.
history: Little is documented about when this tea first appeared or how it has changed. It is known as a Dayi product, but no first release year can be confirmed.
